title: Linux Control Groups (cgroups): The Complete Guide
description: A comprehensive end-to-end guide to Linux control groups. Covers what cgroups are, how they limit and isolate resource usage, cgroup v1 vs v2, managing CPU/memory/IO controllers with systemd and the cgroup filesystem, a hands-on lab from zero to limits, real-world use cases in Docker and Kubernetes, and troubleshooting common issues.
author: E-Learning Platform
heroAlt: Linux cgroups architecture diagram showing resource controllers limiting CPU, memory, and IO for isolated process groups with systemd and Docker integration

sections.title: 1. Introduction to Linux Control Groups
sections.description: What cgroups are and why every DevOps engineer should understand them.
content: Linux control groups (cgroups) are the fundamental resource-isolation building block of containers. Every Docker container, every Kubernetes pod, and every systemd service relies on cgroups to limit, account for, and isolate the resource usage (CPU, memory, disk I/O, network) of a collection of processes. Understanding them is essential for debugging OOM kills, tuning performance, designing multi-tenant systems, and building your own container runtimes from scratch.

A cgroup is a Linux kernel feature that groups processes and applies resource limits to that group as a whole. Each cgroup gets its own view of how much CPU, memory, and I/O it may consume. Processes inside a cgroup share the limits of that group  they are constrained even though the host may have far more resources available.
This guide takes you from zero to a deep understanding of cgroups  with theory, practical commands, and a complete hands-on lab.

items.label: Prerequisites
text: A Linux machine (physical, VM, or cloud instance) with root/sudo access
A kernel from the last decade (cgroup v2 is default on most modern distros)
systemd installed (most distros use systemd as the cgroup manager)
Basic familiarity with the Linux command line
No Docker or containers required  we work with raw cgroups

items.label: What You Will Learn
text: What cgroups are and how they isolate resource usage
How to create, manage, and inspect cgroups with systemd and the cgroupfs
How the CPU, memory, and IO controllers work
How to set hard and soft limits on CPU and memory
How Docker and Kubernetes use cgroups in production
How to troubleshoot OOM kills and CPU throttling
How to debug common cgroup configuration issues

infoBox.content: cgroups are one of the seven Linux namespace types' siblings for isolation. While namespaces isolate WHAT a process can see (network, mounts, PIDs), cgroups isolate HOW MUCH of a resource a process can USE (CPU, memory, IO).

sections.title: 2. What Are Control Groups?
sections.description: Deep dive into kernel-level resource isolation.

infoBox.content: Think of a cgroup as a resource budget for a group of processes. It has its own CPU quota, memory cap, and IO bandwidth  completely isolated from the host's total capacity.

rows: A cgroup can be capped to a fraction of one core or many cores; throttled when over quota
A cgroup can be capped to a max memory; the OOM killer reclaims or kills within the group
Read/write bandwidth and IOPS per device can be throttled per cgroup
cgroups v2 have no native net controller; use TC (traffic control) or namespaces instead
A cgroup can limit how many processes/threads it may spawn (fork bomb protection)
A cgroup can allow/deny access to specific device nodes (e.g., /dev/sda)

items.label: What Is NOT Limited
text: Filesystem contents (that's the mount namespace  CLONE_NEWNS)
Network visibility (that's the network namespace  CLONE_NEWNET)
Process IDs seen by the group (that's the PID namespace  CLONE_NEWPID)
Kernel itself  all cgroups share the same kernel (no hypervisor)
Hardware  physical devices are shared, but access can be denied per cgroup

items.label: Default State of a Fresh Cgroup
text: When you create a new cgroup, it starts with inherited limits from its parent:
No CPU limit  the group may use all available CPU by default
No memory limit  the group may use all available memory by default
No IO limit  the group may use all disk bandwidth by default
Inherited controllers  child cgroups enable the same controllers as the parent
No processes  the cgroup is empty until you add a PID
This empty state is the starting point. Limits must be explicitly configured. You can start with no limits and tighten them, or set strict caps from the beginning.

subsections.title: Kernel Internals (For the Curious)
subsections.content: Under the hood, the Linux kernel maintains a cgroup hierarchy as a tree of cgroup structures. Each process belongs to exactly one cgroup per hierarchy. When you write to a controller file (e.g., memory.max), the kernel's memory controller updates the page-counter for that cgroup and enforces reclaim when the limit is exceeded. This is structural accounting: the kernel literally tracks bytes per cgroup, not just access control lists.

sections.title: 3. Managing Cgroups with systemd and cgroupfs
sections.description: Creating, inspecting, and configuring cgroups on a systemd host.
content: On a modern systemd host, cgroups are managed through two paths: the systemd API (recommended) and the cgroup filesystem (cgroupfs) at /sys/fs/cgroup. Under the hood, systemd writes to the cgroupfs for you. You rarely need to touch the filesystem directly, but understanding it helps debugging.

rows: Show the cgroup tree (like ls for cgroups)
Show the cgroup a unit belongs to
Start a transient cgroup scope with limits
Start a transient cgroup slice with limits
Change live limits on a unit's cgroup
Show which cgroup a process is in

items.label: Create a Transient Cgroup with systemd-run
items.code:
# Create a scope limited to 0.5 CPU and 100MB memory, run a command in it
user@host:~$ sudo systemd-run --scope -p CPUQuota=50% -p MemoryMax=100M --unit demo bash -c 'stress --cpu 2 --timeout 10'

# Inspect the new scope
user@host:~$ systemd-cgls /system.slice/demo.scope

# View the live limits written to the cgroupfs
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/demo.scope/cpu.max
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/demo.scope/memory.max

items.label: Inspect an Existing Process
items.code:
# Which cgroup is the current shell in?
user@host:~$ cat /proc/self/cgroup
0::/user.slice/user-1000.slice/session-1.scope

# Which cgroup is a Docker container in?
user@host:~$ cat /proc/$(pgrep -f nginx | head -1)/cgroup
0::/system.slice/docker-<id>.scope

# Show the full cgroup tree
user@host:~$ systemd-cgls --no-pager | head -40

items.label: Manual cgroupfs (Advanced)
items.code:
# Create a cgroup directly on the cgroup v2 filesystem
user@host:~$ sudo mkdir -p /sys/fs/cgroup/demo

# Enable the cpu and memory controllers for this cgroup
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo "+cpu +memory" > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.subtree_control'

# Set limits by writing to controller files
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo 50000 100000 > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cpu.max'   # 50% of one CPU
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo 100M > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.max'        # 100 MB cap

# Move the current shell into the cgroup
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo $$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.procs'

# Verify
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.procs

sections.title: 4. CPU Controller  Limiting Compute
sections.description: How to throttle and weight CPU usage per cgroup.

infoBox.content: The CPU controller in cgroup v2 uses two mechanisms: cpu.max (a hard quota, like a speed limit) and cpu.weight (a relative share, like priority when the system is busy).

items.label: Hard CPU Quota (cpu.max)
text: The cpu.max file takes two values: MAX MICROSECONDS PER PERIOD (default period 100000 us = 100 ms).
50000 100000  means the cgroup may use at most 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms = 50% of one core
200000 100000 means the cgroup may use at most 200 ms per 100 ms = 2 full cores
max (or 0 100000) means no limit
When the cgroup exceeds its quota, the kernel throttles it  processes in the group stop getting CPU until the next period.

items.label: CPU Weight (cpu.weight)
text: cpu.weight is a relative priority from 1 to 10000 (default 100).
When the system is under load and multiple cgroups want CPU, the scheduler divides available time by weight.
A cgroup with weight 200 gets roughly twice the CPU of one with weight 100, but only when contended.
Unlike cpu.max, weight never caps usage  an idle-priority cgroup can still use all CPU if nothing else wants it.

items.label: Examples
items.code:
# Cap a systemd service to 1.5 cores
user@host:~$ sudo systemctl set-property nginx.service CPUQuota=150%

# Cap via cgroupfs directly (150% = 150000 us per 100000 us period)
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo 150000 100000 > /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/nginx.service/cpu.max'

# Give a batch job low priority (weight 20 vs default 100)
user@host:~$ sudo systemd-run --scope -p CPUWeight=20 --unit batch bash -c 'while true; do :; done'

# Verify the quota
user@host:~$ systemctl show nginx.service -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/nginx.service/cpu.max

items.label: Test CPU Throttling
items.code:
# Run a CPU burner inside a 25% quota scope
user@host:~$ sudo systemd-run --scope -p CPUQuota=25% --unit burn bash -c 'taskset -c 0 yes > /dev/null & sleep 5; kill %1'

# Watch throttling counters
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/burn.scope/cpu.stat
# Look for: throttled_usec and nr_throttled
# nr_throttled > 0 means the cgroup hit its quota and was paused

sections.title: 5. Memory Controller  Limiting RAM
sections.description: How to cap memory and survive the OOM killer.

infoBox.content: When a cgroup hits memory.max, the kernel first tries to reclaim (drop caches, move pages to swap). If that fails, the OOM killer terminates the heaviest process INSIDE that cgroup only  not on the whole host.

rows: Hard cap. Exceeding it triggers reclaim then OOM kill
Soft limit. Throttles and reclaims above this, but no OOM kill
Protected floor. Kernel avoids reclaiming below this if possible
Detailed breakdown of cache, anon, swap, etc. (read-only)

items.label: Set Memory Limits
items.code:
# Cap a service at 512 MB with systemd
user@host:~$ sudo systemctl set-property myapp.service MemoryMax=512M

# Cap via cgroupfs
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo 512M > /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/myapp.service/memory.max'

# Set a soft limit (high) to encourage early reclaim
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo 400M > /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/myapp.service/memory.high'

# Watch usage grow
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/myapp.service/memory.current

items.label: Detect OOM Kills
items.code:
# Did the cgroup hit an OOM?
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/myapp.service/memory.events
# oom_kill 5   <- 5 processes were killed inside this cgroup

# Full dmesg evidence
user@host:~$ sudo dmesg | grep -i "out of memory" | tail -5
user@host:~$ sudo dmesg | grep -i "killed process" | tail -5

# memory.stat for pressure
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/myapp.service/memory.stat | grep -E 'anon|file|swap'

items.label: Hands-On: Trigger an OOM
items.code:
# Start a scope capped at 50MB and try to eat 500MB
user@host:~$ sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=50M --unit oomtest bash -c '\
  python3 -c "x=bytearray(500_000_000); input()"'

# In another terminal, watch it die:
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/oomtest.scope/memory.events
# oom_kill 1

# The bash process is killed; systemd reports the scope as failed

sections.title: 6. IO Controller  Limiting Disk Throughput
sections.description: Throttling block device bandwidth per cgroup.
content: The IO controller (io controller) limits read/write throughput and IOPS per block device. It is useful for preventing a noisy neighbor from starving others of disk bandwidth. Limits are set per device using major:minor numbers.

items.label: Throttle a Device
items.code:
# Find the device major:minor for / (usually 8:0 for sda)
user@host:~$ ls -l /dev/sda
# brw-rw---- 1 root disk 8, 0 ...

# Cap the cgroup to 10 MB/s reads and 100 IOPS writes on sda
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo "8:0 rbps=10M wbps=0 wiops=100" > /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/myapp.service/io.max'

# Relative weight instead of hard cap
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo "8:0 50" > /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/myapp.service/io.weight'

# Verify
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/myapp.service/io.max
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/myapp.service/io.stat

sections.title: 7. Hands-On Lab: From Zero to Limits
sections.description: A complete step-by-step lab creating cgroups and observing limits in action.
content: This lab combines everything you've learned into a single, reproducible workflow. Run each command in order on any Linux machine with systemd and cgroup v2.

items.label: Phase 1: Verify cgroup v2
items.code:
# Confirm the host uses cgroup v2 (unified hierarchy)
user@host:~$ stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup
# Expected: cgroup2fs (NOT tmpfs, which would mean v1)

# See which controllers are available at the root
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.controllers
# cpu memory io pids

# Show the root cgroup's enabled subtree controllers
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.subtree_control

items.label: Phase 2: CPU Limit via systemd-run
items.code:
# Start a CPU burner capped at 30% of one core
user@host:~$ sudo systemd-run --scope -p CPUQuota=30% --unit cpulab bash -c '\n  taskset -c 0 yes > /dev/null & echo $! > /tmp/cpulab.pid; sleep 8; kill $(cat /tmp/cpulab.pid)'

# In another terminal, watch the CPU usage
user@host:~$ top -p $(cat /tmp/cpulab.pid)
# The process shows ~30% CPU, not 100%

# Confirm throttling happened
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/cpulab.scope/cpu.stat | grep throttled
# nr_throttled > 0 means it hit the quota

items.label: Phase 3: Memory Limit via systemd-run
items.code:
# Start a scope capped at 80MB and allocate 200MB
user@host:~$ sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=80M --unit memlab bash -c '\n  python3 -c "x=bytearray(200_000_000); input()"'

# Watch it get OOM-killed
user@host:~$ sudo dmesg | tail -3
# Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process ...

# Confirm the kill counter
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/memlab.scope/memory.events
# oom_kill 1

items.label: Phase 4: Manual cgroupfs Group
items.code:
# Create a persistent cgroup for a batch job
user@host:~$ sudo mkdir -p /sys/fs/cgroup/batchjob
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo "+cpu +memory" > /sys/fs/cgroup/batchjob/cgroup.subtree_control'
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo 100000 100000 > /sys/fs/cgroup/batchjob/cpu.max'  # 1 core
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo 256M > /sys/fs/cgroup/batchjob/memory.max'

# Run a process inside it
user@host:~$ sudo sh -c 'echo $$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/batchjob/cgroup.procs; exec stress --cpu 4 --vm 1 --vm-bytes 200M --timeout 10'

# Inspect
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/batchjob/cgroup.procs
user@host:~$ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/batchjob/memory.current

# Clean up
user@host:~$ sudo rmdir /sys/fs/cgroup/batchjob

items.label: Cleanup Everything
items.code:
# Stop any running scopes
user@host:~$ sudo systemctl stop cpulab.scope memlab.scope 2>/dev/null

# Remove manual cgroups
user@host:~$ sudo rmdir /sys/fs/cgroup/batchjob 2>/dev/null

# Verify the tree is clean
user@host:~$ systemd-cgls --no-pager | head -20
# Expected: no demo/cpulab/memlab/batchjob scopes remain

sections.title: 8. Real-World Use Cases
sections.description: How cgroups power Docker, Kubernetes, systemd, and more.

items.label: Docker Containers
text: Every Docker container gets its own cgroup. When you run docker run, Docker Engine configures cgroups internally:
1. Docker creates a cgroup at /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-<id>.scope
2. It writes cpu.max / cpu.weight based on --cpus and --cpu-shares
3. It writes memory.max based on --memory
4. It writes io.max based on --device-read-bps / --device-write-bps
5. It moves the container's init PID into the cgroup
6. If the container exceeds --memory, the in-cgroup OOM killer fires (not the host)
Example: docker run -d --name web --cpus=1.5 --memory=512m nginx

items.label: Kubernetes Pods
text: In Kubernetes, the kubelet sets cgroup limits from the pod's resources requests/limits:
1. The pod's containers share a cgroup parent (usually kubepods.slice)
2. Each container gets a child cgroup with cpu.max and memory.max
3. The pod-level cgroup sums the container limits (plus overhead)
4. When a container exceeds its memory limit, the in-cgroup OOM killer terminates it
5. The kubelet detects the OOM and marks the container CrashLoopBackOff
6. CPU limits cause throttling (nr_throttled increments) but not termination
This means: a misconfigured limit in Kubernetes maps directly to a cgroup file  understanding cgroups explains pod evictions and throttling.

items.label: systemd Services
text: systemd uses cgroups for every service unit by default. You can set limits in the unit file:
[Service]
CPUQuota=150%
MemoryMax=512M
IOWeight=200
TasksMax=256
This protects the host from a runaway service without containers at all  a best practice for bare-metal servers.

items.label: Fork Bomb Protection
text: cgroups can cap the number of processes (PIDs) a group may spawn, preventing fork bombs from taking down the host:
TasksMax=100  in a systemd unit, or
echo 100 > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/pids.max  on the cgroupfs
When a cgroup hits pids.max, fork() returns EAGAIN  the bomb is contained to that group.

sections.title: 9. Troubleshooting Common Issues
sections.description: Diagnose and fix the most frequent cgroup problems.

infoBox.content: When debugging cgroup issues, always check memory.events for oom_kill and cpu.stat for nr_throttled first. These two counters resolve 90% of resource-limit problems.

items.label: Issue 1: Process Killed Unexpectedly (OOM)
text: Symptoms: a process dies with no error, or a container restarts in a loop
Causes and fixes:
Memory limit too low  raise memory.max / --memory
Memory leak  the process genuinely needs more; profile it
No swap configured  the kernel can't offload pages; add swap or raise the limit
Hit pids.max instead  check memory.events vs pids.events
Diagnostic: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../memory.events | grep oom_kill

items.label: Issue 2: CPU Throttling (Slow But Alive)
text: Symptoms: a CPU-bound job runs much slower than expected but never dies
Causes and fixes:
CPUQuota too low  raise cpu.max / --cpus
Competing cgroups with higher weight  the scheduler favors them under load
Wrong period assumption  remember cpu.max is MAX per 100000 us period
Diagnostic: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../cpu.stat | grep -E 'throttled|nr_throttled'

items.label: Issue 3: Controller Not Available
text: Symptoms: writing to memory.max fails with 'No such file or directory' or 'Permission denied'
Causes and fixes:
Controller not enabled in subtree_control  run: echo +memory > /sys/fs/cgroup/parent/cgroup.subtree_control
On cgroup v1, the path differs (/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/...)  check stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup
Delegated cgroup (rootless container)  you can only enable controllers the parent allows
Docker not mounting the controller  ensure --memory is passed so Docker enables memory

items.label: Issue 4: Limits Don't Apply
text: Symptoms: you set a limit but the process ignores it
Causes and fixes:
Wrong cgroup  you wrote to the parent, not the leaf where the PID lives. Check: cat /proc/<pid>/cgroup
Thread vs process  cgroup.procs moves the whole thread group; use cgroup.threads for individual threads
systemd override conflict  a unit file or drop-in resets the property. Check: systemctl show <unit> -p MemoryMax
Inheritance  child cgroups inherit limits only at creation; existing children keep old values

items.label: Issue 5: cgroup v1 vs v2 Confusion
text: Symptoms: commands from a tutorial don't work on your machine
Cause: your distro uses cgroup v1 (separate hierarchies) while the tutorial assumes v2 (unified).
Check: stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup
cgroup2fs  → v2 (use cpu.max, memory.max, io.max)
tmpfs      → v1 (use /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.cfs_quota_us, /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.limit_in_bytes)
Fix: switch the boot param to v2 (systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=1) or follow v1 syntax.

sections.title: 10. Summary and Next Steps
sections.description: Key takeaways and what to explore next.

items.label: Key Takeaways
text: cgroups limit, account for, and isolate resource usage (CPU, memory, IO, PIDs, devices)
cgroup v2 uses a unified hierarchy with controller files like cpu.max, memory.max, io.max
CPU can be capped (cpu.max) or weighted (cpu.weight)
Memory has hard (memory.max) and soft (memory.high) limits; exceeding hard triggers OOM kill in-group
IO limits are per-block-device using major:minor numbers
systemd-run and systemctl set-property are the easy, safe way to manage cgroups
Docker containers and Kubernetes pods each get their own cgroup  limits map directly to cgroup files
Troubleshooting: check memory.events (oom_kill) and cpu.stat (nr_throttled) first

rows: Set CPU quota on a unit
Set memory cap on a unit

items.label: What to Explore Next
text: Now that you understand cgroups, here are natural next topics to explore:
Docker Deep Dive  how --cpus, --memory, and --pids-limit map to cgroup files
Kubernetes Resource Management  requests vs limits, QoS classes, and OOM eviction
systemd Unit Tuning  CPUAffinity, MemoryZSwap, and IODeviceWeight in unit files
eBPF and BPF Controllers  modern replacements for some cgroup accounting
Pressure Stall Information (PSI)  detecting memory/IO/CPU pressure before OOM
cgroup v1 Internals  the legacy per-controller hierarchies and why v2 replaced them
NRI and crun  how runtimes configure cgroups for containers
The foundation you've built here applies directly to all of these  every container runtime builds on Linux cgroups.
